saint.death_location: The Portiuncula (Santa Maria degli Angeli), near Assisi, Italy
saint.patron: Italy (with St. Catherine of Siena; Pius XII, 18 June 1939); those who promote ecology (John Paul II, Inter Sanctos, 29 November 1979)
saint.relic_description:
Francis died at the Portiuncula, near Assisi, at nightfall on 3 October 1226, and the next day his body was carried to Assisi and buried in the church of San Giorgio; Jordan of Giano says the people feared that Perugia would seize it. On 25 May 1230 (21 May in the 1868 English Bonaventure; the Catholic Encyclopedia’s article on Elias puts it a few days before 25 May) it was moved to the new church built by Brother Elias. According to a papal bull and the account printed by the annalist Wadding, the town’s rulers took the body into their own hands at the church, and it was buried far down beneath the high altar, where its place was forgotten.

After failed searches in 1755 and 1802, a new search allowed by Pope Pius VII found it on 12 December 1818, after fifty-two nights of digging through rock: a Roman travertine sarcophagus inside an iron cage, holding his remains, which Key to Umbria calls essentially intact, with a rough stone for a pillow, a few coins, small beads, and a silver ring with a carnelian cut with Minerva (since lost). A crypt was built beneath the Lower Basilica of San Francesco. In 1934 the remains of Brothers Leo, Masseo, Rufino, and Angelo were moved into niches in the crypt wall, and the casket of Jacoba dei Settesoli to the stairs that lead down to it. An examination allowed by Paul VI in 1978 found a man about 1.57–1.58 m tall. From 21 February to 22 March 2026 the remains were shown in the lower church in the first public and prolonged exposition, and the Franciscans reported more than 350,000 pilgrims.

Robinson (1906) knew of two writings in his own hand. The parchment he wrote for Brother Leo on La Verna in 1224, with the Praises of God and a blessing, is kept at the Sacro Convento in Assisi, where the convent’s records have mentioned it since 1348. A short letter to Leo is kept in the cathedral of Spoleto. Robinson wrote in 1906 that the original bull of 1223 confirming his Rule was kept at the Sacro Convento. Celano reports that, within three years of his death, the bolster Francis used in his sickness and pieces of his girdle were venerated as relics.

Sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Francis of Assisi”; Jordan of Giano, Chronica §50; Wadding, Annales Minorum, vol. 2; Key to Umbria, “San Francesco: Crypt” (facts only); OFM Conv., news pages of 23 February and 25 March 2026 (facts only); Paschal Robinson, The Writings of Saint Francis of Assisi (1906), pp. 64, 130, 146; Thomas of Celano, First Life, §120.
saint.relic_location: Crypt of the Lower Basilica of San Francesco, Assisi, Italy

miracles.miracles:
This list gathers the healings, visions, and other wonders attributed to St. Francis of Assisi, with their sources and their status. When Pope Gregory IX canonized Francis in 1228, his bull Mira circa nos spoke of “many brilliant miracles” but named none. The first group below is the list that Thomas of Celano, his first biographer, says was read aloud before the Pope at the canonization, after the cardinals had heard and examined the miracles brought to them. The bull names none of them, so we cannot say which ones the Church formally approved. The other accounts come from the early Lives (Celano, 1228–29 and 1244–47; the Legend of the Three Companions, 1246; Bonaventure, 1260s) or from later collections (the Mirror of Perfection, about 1318, and the Little Flowers, after 1322), and each entry says which. The list makes no claim of scientific proof, and it does not dismiss any account. Where a story is late, legendary, or was doubted, the entry says so.

Miracles read at the canonization, 1228

A girl with a bent neck, Assisi, 1226

On the day Francis was buried, a girl whose neck was bent was healed beneath his coffin. Celano puts her first in his list of the miracles at the tomb.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §127, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

A boy of Narni who walked on two sticks

A boy of Narni, one of whose legs was bent, could walk only on two sticks. Celano records him among those healed through Francis after his death.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §128, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Nicholas of Foligno, whose leg was drawn up

Nicholas, a man of Foligno, had his left leg drawn up and screamed with pain at night. He had spent his money on doctors. Celano records his healing.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §129, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

A boy bent double

A boy whose knee was drawn up to his breast and whose heel touched his buttocks was healed, Celano says.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §130, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

A man of Fano refused by the hospital

A man of Fano with ulcerated legs, whom the hospital refused to take in, was healed.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §131, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

A girl of Gubbio with contracted hands

A girl of Gubbio whose hands were contracted was healed after eight days. Celano mentions a waxen image in her story.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §132, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

The boy of Montenero and the pears

At the tomb a crippled boy from Montenero was offered pears by a young friar, who then vanished. The boy ate one and was healed.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §133, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Carried in baskets: a woman and a boy

A woman of Coccorano and the son of a citizen of Gubbio were both carried in baskets, and Celano records both as healed.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §134, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Bartholomew of Narni and the bath

Bartholomew of Narni, a bent beggar, was told in a dream to go to a bath. On the way he lost the road at night, and a voice put him right. Celano records his healing.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §135, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Six blind people given sight

Celano lists a woman named Sibyl, a man of Spello, a woman of Camerino who was healed with a cloth Francis had touched, a woman of Gubbio, and Albertino of Narni. The sixth was a citizen of Assisi, blind for five years, who had been a close friend of Francis.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §136, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Peter of Foligno, troubled for three years

Peter of Foligno had drunk from a spring on the way to the shrine of Monte Sant’Angelo, and for three years he was troubled by demons. Celano records that he was freed.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §137, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

A woman of Narni, and Celano’s caution

A woman of Narni was freed after Francis appeared to her in a vision and signed her with the cross. Celano himself adds that people of that kind “are often the victims of delusion,” and he moves on.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §138, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Matthew of Todi: “Ciccu, Ciccu”

The boy Matthew of Todi, whose skin had turned black, was healed after his mother made a vow to Francis. Celano records that the child lisped “Ciccu, Ciccu.”

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §139, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Falls and injuries: a speechless lad, Mancino, Walter of Arezzo

A lad who fell from a height and could not speak for three days was healed. Celano lists with him a man named Mancino and Walter of Arezzo, whose story mentions a waxen image.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §140, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

A withered hand, dropsy, and gout

Celano records the healing of a withered hand at Narni, of dropsy at Fano, and of gout at Todi.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §141, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Bontadoso, who did not believe

A man named Bontadoso said of Francis, “I don’t believe he is a Saint.” When he fell ill, he made a vow: “I vow myself to Saint Francis, and believe him to be a Saint, if he cures me of this illness within three days.” Celano records that he was cured.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §142, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

An iron arrowhead in the eye socket

A man had an iron arrowhead lodged in his eye socket. Francis appeared to him in a dream and told him to have it removed through the back of the head, and the man recovered.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §143, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Imperatore of Spello and a friar with a fistula

Imperatore of Spello was healed of a rupture. A friar with a fistula was told to throw away his fur coat and his plaster, and was healed.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §144–145, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Two lepers: Atto of San Severino and Bonuomo of Fano

Celano records the healing of two lepers, Atto of San Severino and Bonuomo of Fano. His account of Atto mentions a candle of Atto’s own height offered each year.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §146, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

The deaf and mute boy of Castel della Pieve

A boy of Castel della Pieve who could neither hear nor speak, and whose tongue seemed to have been cut off, began to speak. His first words were “Saint Francis lives,” and “I see Saint Francis standing up there.”

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §147, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

The last cures in Celano’s list

Celano ends his list with a cure at Villa, a man near Perugia who vomited blood, a woman with a stone in her throat, and a boy of Greccio.

Status: read before Pope Gregory IX at the canonization in 1228, according to Celano. The bull of canonization names no miracle.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §147–150, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

During Francis’s life

The crucifix that spoke, San Damiano, about 1205–06

While Francis prayed in the ruined church of San Damiano, the painted crucifix spoke to him: “Francis, seest thou not that My House is being destroyed? Go therefore, and repair Me it.” In Celano’s Second Life the image moved its lips and called him by name. Celano’s First Life tells of his visit to the church but says nothing of a voice.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Legend of the Three Companions, 1246; Celano, Second Life, 1244–47); not in the earliest Life.

Source: Legend of the Three Companions, §13, tr. E. G. Salter, 1902, https://archive.org/details/legendofsaintfra00unse

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life, §10, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Pope Innocent III’s dream of the Lateran, about 1209–10

Before he approved the brothers’ way of life, Innocent III had dreamed that the Lateran basilica was leaning as if to fall, and that a small religious man was holding it up with his back.

Status: reported only in the Legend of the Three Companions (1246).

Source: Legend of the Three Companions, §51, tr. E. G. Salter, 1902, https://archive.org/details/legendofsaintfra00unse

Silvester’s dream of a cross

The priest Silvester, who had complained that Francis underpaid him for stones, later dreamed that a huge cross grew out of Francis’s mouth, and he joined the brothers.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Legend of the Three Companions; Bonaventure alludes to it).

Source: Legend of the Three Companions, §30–31, tr. E. G. Salter, 1902, https://archive.org/details/legendofsaintfra00unse

Water into wine at Sant’Urbano

At Sant’Urbano near Narni, when Francis was ill, water was turned into wine, and he was cured by tasting it.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, First Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §61, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

The sermon to the birds, near Bevagna

Near Bevagna Francis came upon a gathering of birds, doves and rooks and others, and went among them, touching them with his tunic. He told them, “My brother birds, much ought ye to praise your Creator, and ever to love Him who has given you feathers for clothing, wings for flight, and all that ye had need of.” The birds listened and spread their wings.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, First Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §58, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

The swallows of Alviano

At Alviano the swallows were so noisy that Francis could not preach. “My sisters, the swallows, it is now time for me to speak too, because you have been saying enough all this time,” he told them. “Listen to the word of God and be in silence, and quiet, until the sermon is finished!” They were quiet.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, First Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §59, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

A hare at Greccio and a fish near Rieti

At Greccio a young hare ran into Francis’s lap. Near Rieti a tench stayed beside his boat until he had finished praying.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, First Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §60–61, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Healings at Ascoli

At Ascoli, Celano says, bread that Francis had blessed healed the sick, and so did his clothes and cords.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, First Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §62–64, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Horse reins for a woman in labor, near Arezzo

Near Arezzo a woman in a hard labor was delivered after the reins of a horse Francis had held were placed on her.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, First Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §63, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

A falcon that woke him for prayer

A falcon used to wake Francis for the night Office, Bonaventure says, and when Francis was sick it woke him later.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Bonaventure).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 8, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

A spring from the rock for a thirsty muleteer

Francis had borrowed a poor man’s ass, and on the mountain the man collapsed with thirst. Francis knelt to pray and sent him to a rock where, Bonaventure says, “never was flowing water in that place before.” Celano’s Second Life tells the same story and adds that no water could be found there afterward, “as diligent search has proved.”

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life §46; Bonaventure).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 6, “Love of Poverty”, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

Fire that did not burn

Before a surgeon cauterized his face from the ear to the eyebrow for his eye disease, Francis spoke to the fire: “Be kind to me at this hour, be courteous, for I have loved thee of old in the Lord.” The brothers fled. When they came back he told them, “I felt no heat of fire nor any pain in my flesh,” and the surgeon said, “I have seen wondrous things to-day.”

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life §166, with the surgeon and brothers as witnesses; Bonaventure).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §166, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 5, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

The child in the manger, Greccio, Christmas 1223

At the Christmas Mass sung over a manger at Greccio, one man saw a lifeless child lying in the manger and saw Francis wake it. Celano does not name the man; Bonaventure says it was the knight John of Greccio. Celano adds that hay from the manger later cured sick animals and eased women in labor.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, First Life; Bonaventure. The vision rests on one witness).

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §84–87, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. X, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

The stigmata, La Verna, 1224

Two years before his death, on La Verna, Francis saw a six-winged seraph fixed to a cross, and marks of nails appeared in his hands and feet, with a wound in his right side that bled. He hid them; Brother Rufino touched the side wound by accident, and Elias saw it. Bonaventure dates the vision about the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross and says that more than fifty brothers, Clare and her sisters, cardinals, and Pope Alexander IV saw the wounds. The bull of canonization does not mention them, and Bonaventure’s own stories show that some doubted them in the thirteenth century.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, First Life; Bonaventure); contested then; venerated in the Catholic Church.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §94–96, 112–113, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 13, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

The Gospel opened three times at the Passion

On La Verna, before the vision, Francis opened the Gospel book three times, and each time it opened at the Passion of Christ.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Bonaventure).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 13, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

Warm on the mountain

Bonaventure says that after Francis received the stigmata the snow and rocks of the mountain did not chill him.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Bonaventure).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 13, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

Hail stopped at La Verna

After the vision on La Verna, Bonaventure says, the hail stopped.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Bonaventure).

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. XIII.7, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

A plague of sheep and oxen ended, Rieti

At Rieti a plague among the sheep and oxen ended through the water in which Francis’s hands and feet had been washed.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Bonaventure).

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. XIII.6, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

A poor man warmed on a winter night

On a winter night under a rock, Bonaventure says, Francis’s touch took the cold away from a poor man who was with him.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Bonaventure).

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. XIII.7, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

Leo’s temptation and the parchment, La Verna, 1224

Brother Leo was struggling with a temptation. Francis wrote out for him the Praises of God and a blessing on one parchment and told him to keep it until his death, and the temptation left Leo at once. The parchment survives at the Sacro Convento in Assisi.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life, as quoted in Paschal Robinson, The Writings of Saint Francis of Assisi, 1906, p. 146, https://archive.org/details/cu31924029364787

Brother Pacifico’s vision of swords

Pacifico, a poet once crowned “King of Verses,” met Francis at a convent of nuns in the March of Ancona and saw him signed as with a cross by two glittering swords. He joined the brothers the next day. Later he saw a Tau on Francis’s forehead.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life §106, from Pacifico’s own account; Bonaventure).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §106, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. XIII.10, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

Elias’s vision at Foligno

At Foligno, Elias saw an aged priest dressed in white, who told him that eighteen years had passed since Francis’s conversion, and that Francis would live two more.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, First Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §108, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

The Lady Jacoba’s arrival, 1226

As Francis lay dying, the brothers wrote to the Lady Jacoba dei Settesoli to ask for cloth and almond cakes. She arrived with exactly those things before the letter was sent, as if prompted in spirit.

Status: late account (Mirror of Perfection, about 1318).

Source: The Mirror of Perfection, “Of the food and cloth he desired before his death,” 1902 English tr., https://archive.org/details/TheMirrorOfPerfection

The wolf of Gubbio

The Little Flowers tells how Francis met a wolf at Gubbio and commanded it: “Come hither, brother wolf: I command thee in the name of Christ that thou do no harm, nor to me nor to any one.”

Status: legendary (Little Flowers, compiled after 1322; earliest dated manuscript 1390).

Source: The Little Flowers of Saint Francis, ch. XXI, tr. T. W. Arnold, https://archive.org/details/littleflowersofs00arno

At Francis’s death, 3 October 1226

His soul seen as a star

One of the brothers saw Francis’s soul rise to heaven like a star, as large as the moon, carried on a white cloud.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, First Life; Bonaventure).

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §110, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Larks on the roof

At the hour of his death the larks, “birds that love the light, and dread the shades of twilight,” came in great numbers to the roof of the house. The Mirror of Perfection puts it on the Saturday evening after vespers and says they wheeled in a circle round the roof, singing.

Status: reported in Bonaventure and in the Mirror of Perfection (late).

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. CXIII, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. XIV.6, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

Brother Augustine’s cry and the bishop’s vision

At that hour Brother Augustine, minister of the brothers in the Terra di Lavoro, who was dying and had long since lost his speech, cried out, “Wait for me, father, wait! See, I am now coming with thee!” The bishop of Assisi, returning from the shrine of Monte Sant’Angelo on Monte Gargano, saw Francis that same night, and had a notary write down the day and hour.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life §218–220; Bonaventure).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §218–220, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. XIV.6, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

The body after death, and the knight Jerome

Brother Elias, writing within days, says that Francis’s body, rigid and marked by suffering in life, became after death very beautiful, shining with whiteness, and its stiff limbs became soft “like those of tender children” (our translation from the Latin). Celano and Bonaventure agree: after his death Francis’s flesh was white and his limbs soft, the nail marks black, “formed out of his flesh,” and the side red; Bonaventure compares it to “a rose most fair.” At Assisi a knight named Jerome, who doubted, moved the nails with his own fingers in front of his fellow citizens and then swore to it on the Gospels.

Status: reported by Elias’s letter of October 1226 and the early Lives (Celano, First Life; Bonaventure).

Source: Brother Elias, letter to the provinces, 1226, in Wadding, Annales Minorum, vol. 2 (1732), pp. 149–150 (page scan checked), https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_3Dn8hVWLUNwC

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §112–113, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

More accounts from Celano’s Second Life and the Mirror of Perfection

These accounts were added after a second reading of Celano’s Second Life (1244–47) and the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318). Celano names a witness for some of them; the Mirror is late and is marked so.

The leper who vanished

After Francis got down from his horse and kissed the leper, Celano’s Second Life says, he mounted again and looked round, and there was no leper anywhere on the open plain.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life only; Francis’s own Testament tells the meeting without this detail).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §9, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

The defeat at Damietta foretold, 29 August 1219

In the crusader camp before Damietta, Francis warned that if the army fought on a certain day it would lose. The soldiers laughed at him, attacked, and were routed; Celano counts six thousand killed and captured.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life. Jacques de Vitry, who was in the crusader camp, also places Francis there).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §30, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Brother Leonard’s thought

On the road home from the East, Francis, riding an ass, got down at the very moment Brother Leonard was resenting, in silence, that the son of a merchant rode while he walked, and said it was not right that he should ride while Leonard went on foot.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life; in Celano’s telling, Leonard himself confessed his thought to Francis).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §31, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Wolves and hail at Greccio

Francis promised the people of Greccio that if they confessed and changed their lives, the wolves and hailstorms that troubled them would stop. They did, Celano says, until the town fell back into its old ways.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life; a moral tale in Celano’s telling).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §35–36, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Civil strife at Perugia foretold

Francis rebuked the people of Perugia for the evil they had done to their neighbors and warned them of what would follow; Celano says civil war broke out in the city days later. The Mirror of Perfection repeats the story.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life; Mirror of Perfection).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §37, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Canon Gideon of Rieti

At Rieti, during his last illness, a dissolute canon named Gideon begged for the sign of the cross. Francis rebuked him, then blessed him, and Gideon was healed; Celano adds that he later died when a roof fell on him.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life; with a moral of Celano’s own).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §41, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

The nail parings

A brother of the Marsica, tormented by temptation, asked for Francis’s nail parings. Francis called for scissors at once and gave them to him, and the temptation left him.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §42, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

The doctor’s dinner at Rieti

Francis told the brothers to give the eye doctor a good dinner, though they had almost nothing. A woman came to the door with a basket of fine bread, fish, crayfish pasties, honey, and grapes; the Mirror says she was sent by the lady of a castle. The doctor told the brothers that neither they nor the world knew Francis’s holiness as they ought.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life, with the doctor as witness; the Mirror of Perfection places it at Fonte Colombo).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §44, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. CX, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

Cloth for six tunics

Francis asked his warden for cloth for one tunic, and a man at the gate offered cloth for six. “Thanks be to Him who seems to take thought for us alone!” Francis said.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §43, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Parsley in the dark

During his last illness the cook said he could not find parsley in the dark. Francis told him to bring the first herbs he touched, and among the wild herbs there was a leaf of parsley.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §51, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A famine foretold, and a visit after death

Francis told a brother that God would not allow famine on the earth while a certain servant of his lived. After Francis’s death he appeared to the same brother to say that the famine was now coming, and Celano writes that he and others witnessed the famine that followed.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §52–53, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

“Welcome, Lady Poverty!”

On the road from Rieti to Siena to have his eyes treated, Francis met three poor women, who greeted him, “Welcome, Lady Poverty!” and then vanished. Celano calls it “a wondrous thing, of doubtful interpretation, but most certain truth.”

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life; the physician and brothers were with him).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §93, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

The bishop who could not speak

Bishop Guido of Assisi once walked into Francis’s cell at the Portiuncula unannounced, and found himself trembling, unable to speak, and driven backward. His speech came back when he confessed his fault.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §100, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Warmth felt from afar

The abbot of San Giustino near Perugia asked Francis to pray for him. Francis stopped to pray, and the abbot, already some distance away, felt a sudden warmth.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §101, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Demons driven from Arezzo

When Arezzo was torn by civil war, Francis saw demons over the city and sent Brother Silvester to the gate to order them out in God’s name and his. Peace returned.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §108, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

The sow and the lamb

Near Gubbio a sow killed a newborn lamb. Francis grieved for it and cursed the sow, which sickened and died within three days.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life; a harsh tale, not the wolf of Gubbio).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §111, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

The lute at Rieti

Ill at Rieti, Francis asked a brother to borrow a lute to soothe him, but the brother was afraid of what people would say. That night a lute was heard playing in the room, with no player to be seen.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §126, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A waterfowl, bees, a pheasant, and a cicada

A waterfowl given to Francis on the lake of Rieti stayed in his open hands while he prayed. A pheasant sent to him kept returning to his cell and would not eat away from him. Bees filled the cup he had used during a forty-day fast. A cicada on a fig tree near the Portiuncula came when he called her and sang with him, and stayed eight days until he gave her leave to go.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §167–171, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A hood saved from the fire, and bones on the altar

A brother’s hood thrown into a large fire was pulled out unharmed at Francis’s word. At Monte Casale, when the brothers neglected to move relics as he had told them, they later found the bones laid on the altar.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, Second Life; of legendary character).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §154, §202, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A purse that became a snake, and a capon that became a fish

Near Bari, Celano says, a purse of coins that a brother wanted to pick up turned out to hold a snake. At Alessandria a man who kept a piece of capon from Francis’s table to shame him found that it looked to everyone like fish.

Status: of legendary character (Celano, Second Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §68, §78–79, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Peace between the bishop and the governor of Assisi, 1226

When the bishop and the governor of Assisi were at odds, Francis added a verse on pardon to his Canticle and sent two brothers to sing it before them. The governor forgave the bishop at once, and the two embraced.

Status: late account (Mirror of Perfection, compiled about 1318, from older memories of the companions).

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. CI, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

The priest’s vineyard at Rieti

A priest near Rieti complained that visitors to Francis had ruined his vineyard. Francis promised him that it would yield at least twenty measures of wine, and it did.

Status: late account (Mirror of Perfection, compiled about 1318, from older memories of the companions).

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. CIV, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

Chub in winter, and the bread that healed

Lying ill in the bishop’s palace, Francis said he could eat a little chub, and three large ones arrived from Rieti, though it was winter. A brother kept a morsel of the bread Francis blessed and shared before his death, and the Mirror says many sick people were healed after tasting it.

Status: late account (Mirror of Perfection, compiled about 1318, from older memories of the companions).

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. CXI, LXXXVIII, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

After Francis’s death: other accounts

The bolster and the girdle, France and elsewhere

Within three years of the death, Celano wrote that in France “the king and queen and all the magnates ran to kiss and worship the bolster which Saint Francis had used in his sickness,” and that people were cured by pieces of his girdle.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Celano, First Life).

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §120, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Pope Gregory IX’s dream of the side wound

Pope Gregory IX, Bonaventure says, “felt some doubt and hesitation of mind with regard to the wound in the side.” Francis appeared to him in a dream, stern, lifted his arm, showed the wound, and told him to fill a vessel with its blood, and the Pope held it full to the brim. Gregory told the story, Bonaventure says, with many tears.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Bonaventure).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

A doubting friar who washed the saint’s feet

A friar who preached and who doubted the stigmata saw Francis in a vision with muddy feet. He washed them and touched the places of the nails.

Status: reported in Bonaventure; of legendary character.

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

John of Ilerda, stabbed

In Ilerda in Catalonia a man named John was stabbed so deeply that the matter from the wound put out six candles. Francis, in a friar’s habit, came in by the window and unwrapped his bandages, and John was healed.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Bonaventure).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

Roger of Potenza and the wounded palm

Roger, a canon of Potenza, doubted the stigmata as he looked at a picture of Francis, and he received a wound like an arrow’s in his palm. He was healed after he confessed. Bonaventure says the account was authenticated by the bishop’s seal.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Bonaventure; the seal is mentioned only by him).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

The Roman lady’s picture

A woman of Rome saw the stigmata appear on a painted portrait of Francis. When she doubted, they vanished.

Status: legendary (reported in Bonaventure).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

“Many” raised from the dead

Bonaventure claims that many were raised from the dead through Francis. The sources read for this list give no names.

Status: reported in the early Lives (Bonaventure; no named cases read).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

teachings.teachings:
Francis wrote little, and simply. His Rules, his Testament, a handful of letters, short sayings called Admonitions, and his songs of praise survive. The passages below are our own English translations: the Latin from the 1904 Quaracchi critical edition, and the Canticle from the thirteenth-century Assisi manuscript. The Testament, the letter to Leo, the Praises, and the last will for Clare were checked against page scans of that edition; the other Latin was read in a scanned text. The famous prayer that begins “Lord, make me an instrument of your peace” is not his; it was first printed, unsigned, in Paris in 1912.

What was bitter became sweet

For Francis, conversion began with the thing he could least bear. The Lord “led” him among the lepers, he wrote, and what had been bitter turned into sweetness. His own account puts that change at the root of his new life.

“When I was in sins, it seemed too bitter to me to see lepers. The Lord himself led me among them, and I showed them mercy. And when I left them, what had seemed bitter to me turned into sweetness of soul and body.”

— Francis of Assisi, Testament, 1226 (our translation from the Latin)

He left these words in his Testament, near the end of his life, and put them first, before anything else he wanted his brothers to remember. He lived them: he kissed a leper’s hand on the road, gave alms in the leper house, and near death still wanted to go back and serve the lepers.

The form of the Gospel

Francis believed God had shown him a way of life that was simply the Gospel, lived literally. His brothers were to own nothing, because Christ had made himself poor.

“The Most High himself showed me that I should live according to the form of the holy Gospel. And I had it written in a few words and simply, and the lord pope confirmed it for me.”

— Francis of Assisi, Testament, 1226 (our translation from the Latin)

In the Rule of 1223 he wrote: “The brothers shall make nothing their own, not house, nor place, nor anything. … For the Lord made himself poor for us in this world.” He asked that his words be understood “simply and purely,” as they were written. When he heard the Gospel of the sending of the Twelve, he threw away his shoes, staff, and belt, and he died in a habit that had been lent to him.

Brothers who mother each other

Francis asked his brothers to care for each other with a mother’s tenderness, and he used the same image for every Christian who carries Christ in the heart.

“For if a mother feeds and loves her son in the flesh, how much more carefully should one love and feed his spiritual brother?”

— Francis of Assisi, Rule of 1223, ch. 6 (our translation from the Latin)

In his Letter to All the Faithful he wrote: “We are his mothers when we carry him in heart and body through love and a pure and sincere conscience.” In a note to Brother Leo, written in his own hand, he spoke “as a mother would,” and ended: “if you need it for your soul, or for some other comfort, and you want, Leo, to come to me, come.”

Mercy without limit

Francis could be severe with brothers who refused the Rule, but he asked those in charge to be merciful without condition. He told one minister to take whatever stood in his way, even from the brothers, as grace.

“No brother, however much he has sinned, should leave your presence without mercy, if he asks mercy; if he does not ask, you ask him.”

— Francis of Assisi, Letter to a Minister (our translation from the Latin)

He wrote this to a minister whose name the letter does not keep. On his deathbed he forgave all his brothers, “as well absent as present,” as Celano records.

Patience shows what we are

Francis held that a person’s worth is what he is before God, and that patience is tested only when others oppose us.

“You cannot tell how much patience and humility a servant of God has while everything pleases him. But when the people who should satisfy him do the opposite, he has as much patience and humility as he shows then, and no more.”

— Francis of Assisi, Admonition XIII (our translation from the Latin)

In another Admonition he wrote, “As much as a person is before God, so much he is, and no more.” And in another: “Where there is love and wisdom, there is neither fear nor ignorance. Where there is patience and humility, neither anger nor disturbance. Where there is poverty with joy, neither greed nor avarice.” The true peacemakers, he wrote, are those who keep peace in mind and body, whatever they suffer, for the love of Christ.

Praise through the creatures

Francis saw every creature as a brother or sister, and the whole world as a reason to praise God. He preached to birds and spoke to fire as “brother fire.”

“Praised be my Lord for our sister, mother earth, who sustains and governs us and brings forth many fruits with colored flowers and grass.”

— Francis of Assisi, Canticle of Brother Sun, San Damiano, about 1225 (our translation from the Umbrian Italian)

He made the Canticle, ill and nearly blind, in a hut near San Damiano, in the Italian of Umbria rather than Latin. Its last line sums up what he asked of everyone: “Praise and bless my Lord, give him thanks, and serve him with great humility.” Even death was “our sister, bodily death, from whom no living person can escape.”

Work and simplicity

Francis wanted his brothers to work with their hands, and he told those who could not read not to trouble about learning letters but to long for the Spirit of the Lord.

“And I worked with my own hands, and I want to work.”

— Francis of Assisi, Testament, 1226 (our translation from the Latin)

In the Testament he remembered the first days: “we were uneducated and subject to everyone.” The Rule of 1223 asks that preaching be brief and that brothers who cannot read not trouble to learn. He himself carried stones to rebuild San Damiano and begged for what he ate.

Poverty to the end

Francis wanted to follow the poverty that Christ and his mother had lived, and he asked Clare and her sisters never to leave it, whatever anyone advised them.

“I, little Brother Francis, want to follow the life and poverty of our most high Lord Jesus Christ and of his most holy mother, and to hold to it to the end.”

— Francis of Assisi, last will for Clare and her sisters (our translation from the Latin)

He wrote it shortly before he died, and Clare kept it by copying it into her own Rule. In his Testament he wrote of going back to “the Lord’s table,” begging alms from door to door. On his deathbed he would accept his habit only as a loan.

A servant to everyone

Francis called himself the servant of his brothers and of everyone. He gave up the government of the Order in 1220, saying, “Henceforth I am dead to you,” and promised obedience to the man who took his place.

“I think myself the greatest of sinners, for if God had followed any other wicked man with such great mercy he would have been tenfold more spiritual than I.”

— Francis of Assisi, in Thomas of Celano’s Second Life, 1244–47 (tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell)

He signed his letter to all Christians “brother Francis, their servant and subject,” and his Testament “your little one and servant.” When a brother urged him in his illness to have the Prophets read to him, he answered, “I need no more, my son: I know Christ, the poor man crucified.”

did_you_know.fact: Only two pieces of Francis’s own handwriting are known, Paschal Robinson wrote in 1906, and both were written for his friend Brother Leo.
The first announcement of Francis’s stigmata, Brother Elias’s letter of October 1226, mentions no mountain, no seraph, and no date.

The earliest account of Francis’s visit to the Sultan, by Bishop Jacques de Vitry, who was with the crusaders at Damietta, says nothing of a trial by fire; it says the Sultan asked Francis to pray for him.

did_you_know.fact: When his body was found in 1818 after fifty-two nights of digging, a rough stone lay under his head for a pillow.

gaps: Biography is 9,972 words by the lint count (narrative, source note, and research paragraph), within the tier A range.

Latin quoted in the biography is limited to lines checked against page scans (Jacques de Vitry, fol. 353). Francis’s Testament, last will for Clare, Leo letter, and Chartula, and Elias’s letter were checked against scans; Jordan of Giano, Thomas of Spalato, Jacques’s letters, and Wadding’s 1230 bull were read only in OCR and appear in our English without quotation of the Latin. The biography also prints the three-word Latin phrase Secretum meum mihi as it stands in the 1868 English Bonaventure, and the Latin titles of the bulls Solet annuere, Mira circa nos and Speravimus.
The early Lives (Celano, Three Companions, Bonaventure, Mirror, Little Flowers) were read in English translations only.

Not read: Celano’s Treatise on the Miracles, Julian of Speyer’s Life and Office, Bonaventure’s Minor Legend, the Legend of Perugia and Assisi Compilation in Latin, the rest of Jacques de Vitry’s Historia occidentalis, the Latin process of Clare, the bulls of 1237 and 1255 on the stigmata, the 1818 reports and the 1820 bull Assisiensem Basilicam, and modern studies (Tolan, Frugoni, Cooper).

Date conflicts are set out in the biography’s source note: canonization 16 July vs the bull’s dating clause; death at nightfall 3 Oct (Elias: first hour of the night before Sunday 4 Oct); stigmata day; translation 25 vs 21 May 1230 (the Catholic Encyclopedia’s article on Elias puts it a few days before 25 May; a web summary also gives 22 May); the bull Speravimus printed with an impossible date (Key to Umbria gives 16 June 1230); Clare’s flight 1212 vs about 1211.
